auraIntro: Explorer, Black Eye Galaxy features a dramatic dark dust band and counter-rotating gas disks from an ancient collision.
overview: The Black Eye Galaxy (M64) is an isolated spiral galaxy in the constellation Coma Berenices, located approximately 17 million light-years from Earth.
formation: Created by a merger approximately 1 billion years ago when M64 absorbed a gas-rich satellite galaxy rotating in the opposite direction.
structure: A spiral galaxy spanning 40,000 light-years. Remarkably, its outer interstellar gas rotates in the OPPOSITE direction relative to its inner stars and central core.
discoveryHistory: Discovered on March 23, 1779 by Edward Pigott and independently by Johann Elert Bode and Charles Messier.
observationTips: Famous in small telescopes; a 4-inch telescope easily reveals the dark dust patch obscuring the north side of its core.
funFacts: The dark 'eye' feature is a dense band of light-absorbing interstellar dust blocking stars behind the core.
Outer gas cloud rotates counter-clockwise while inner stars rotate clockwise due to an absorbed satellite galaxy.

cards.title: Arrival: The Dark Banded Core
cards.subtitle: Messier 64 Overview
cards.body: Welcome to the Black Eye Galaxy (M64), one of the most enigmatic spiral galaxies in our local universe. Located 17 million light-years away in Coma Berenices, M64 spans 40,000 light-years across. It earns its striking nickname from a dark, heavy band of light-absorbing dust sitting directly in front of its bright central core.

cards.title: Discovery: Pigott, Bode & Messier
cards.subtitle: 18th-Century Observations
cards.body: M64 was discovered independently three times in 1779: first by Edward Pigott on March 23, 1779, then by Johann Elert Bode 12 days later, and cataloged by Charles Messier in 1780. William Herschel noted its dark dust lane in 1785, comparing it to a dark eye staring through space.
bulletPoints: Edward Pigott first discovered M64 on March 23, 1779.
Charles Messier added it as M64 to his catalog in March 1780.
William Herschel mapped the dark obscuring dust cloud in 1785.

cards.title: Cosmic Story: Counter-Rotating Gas Disks
cards.subtitle: Opposing Motions Inside One Galaxy
cards.body: Spectroscopic Doppler velocity measurements revealed an extraordinary kinematic anomaly inside M64: while its inner stellar disk and gas rotate in one direction, the outer gas disk rotates in the exact OPPOSITE direction. Where these opposing gas systems rub together at the boundary, friction compresses gas into a ring of intense star formation.
bulletPoints: Outer gas disk extends from 3,000 to 40,000 light-years, rotating opposite to the core.
Shear boundary between opposing gas flows triggers rapid starbirth.
Young blue star clusters line the active friction boundary ring.

cards.title: Deep Insight: NASA 2026 Multi-Spectrum Image
cards.subtitle: Hubble & Webb Joint Analysis
cards.body: In 2026, NASA released a multi-spectrum image of M64 combining Hubble optical resolution with Webb infrared optics. The composite image penetrates the dark dust lane, revealing the detailed distribution of cold molecular gas and newborn protostars along the shear boundary.
bulletPoints: Hubble optical resolution captures dark dust silhouetting bright core starlight.
Webb mid-infrared optics penetrate dust to reveal hidden embedded protostars.
Multi-spectrum mapping proves counter-rotation is driving active starbursts.

cards.title: Cosmic Curiosity: Evidence of a Cannibalized Satellite
cards.subtitle: 1 Billion Year Ancient Merger
cards.body: How did M64 acquire counter-rotating gas? Astrophysicists conclude that roughly 1 billion years ago, M64 collided with and absorbed a gas-rich satellite dwarf galaxy that was orbiting in the opposite direction. M64 devoured the satellite's stars, but its retrograde gas remains as a smoking gun of ancient galactic cannibalism.
bulletPoints: Counter-rotating gas was donated by a retrogradely orbiting dwarf satellite galaxy.
The dwarf satellite's stars mixed into M64's main disk over 1 billion years.
In a few hundred million years, friction will eventually align all gas in one direction.
